items.title: FCC should focus on robot security, not country of origin
items.summary: The Go2 quadruped robot from Unitree, a prominent Chinese robot developer. | Source: Unitree The FCC is right to treat connected robots as a security issue . Its recent action restricting foreign-produced advanced robotic devices reflects a real risk. These machines carry cameras and sensors, transmit data, take remote software updates, and make their own decisions inside factories, warehouses, stores, and airports. But where a robot was assembled tells you little about who controls it once it's deployed. A robot built entirely in the United States, with unsigned updates and open remote access, is a bigger risk than one built overseas with secure software. The real security boundary is the code, the data, and whoever can change them, not the chassis. The FCC has already recognized this. items.title: Space robotics: notes from an IROS 2026 plenary session
items.summary: By Emmet Cole Space robotics was the focus of a plenary panel at IROS 2026 in Pittsburgh, where speakers from NASA, JAXA and academia discussed the roles robots will play in lunar exploration, human spaceflight and work in orbit. Their examples ranged from unloading cargo and building lunar infrastructure to collecting samples from Phobos and removing space debris. The presentations also pointed to a wider question: how can investment in space robotics advance capabilities that matter on Earth? Rob Ambrose , a professor at Texas A&M and former NASA principal technologist for robotics and autonomy, made that case through the potential links between lunar work and industries such as construction, transport, logistics, mining and solar power. items.title: How DARPA Challenged Teams to Bring Robots Into Disaster Triage
items.summary: On 5 November, 10 teams descended upon a 52-acre mock town in College Station, Texas called Disaster City . They were there for a nine-day competition to see how well teams of robots and humans could navigate simulated catastrophes, like a market ravaged by a tornado and a nighttime strike on a military base. At stake? US $2.5 million in prize money. The scenarios were the final of the DARPA Triage Challenge , which the U.S. agency has been running for three years with the goal of saving more lives in urgent mass casualty events. Engineers from academia and industry have competed in elaborately staged mass casualty events , such as simulated combat zones and plane crash scenes.
